verdicts.note: The 0 reflects real mixed evidence. On the record side: more than 15 years as a career prosecutor, more than 100 jury trials, the office's current chief criminal deputy, and acting duties in Pacific County [S1][S3][S9]. On the renewal side: he has never held elected office [S1], he challenges the incumbent, and he runs on 'restore accountability' [S2]. The 'not politics as usual' line in the scoring notes has no cited position line in the dossier, so the renewal side is a little thinner than the notes suggest. Still 0, at medium.

Several independent sources show it. He promises to 'aggressively pursue' offenders and criticizes repeat offenders 'too often released' [S2]. He said 'we're going to be hard on crime' [S8]. The county administrator credits him with pushing more trials [S8], and his sentencing asks and comments go the same way [S9][S10]. Therapeutic courts for 'the people we can help' [S8] and 'accountability, structure, compassion, and support' [S1] are real counterweights, so -1 rather than -2.

This is one source counted twice. S7 and S8 are two Daily World stories on the same October 2025 pay dispute, where Crawford, as chief criminal deputy under Tillotson, argued for raises for his own staff and for filling vacant positions. That is a department manager advocating for his budget line, not a stated view on government spending, and his campaign materials (S1-S4) say nothing about budgets or spending. The direction is plausible, but the evidence does not support medium confidence.

The direction holds: he is the appointed incumbent with 11 years in the office and four at WAPA [S1][S6], and he runs on stability and training [S4]. High overstates it. He has held the post only since March 2026 and has never won an election [S1]. His opponent is an equally tenured insider, so the record-vs-renewal contrast is narrow. Part of his pitch is fixing the office ('turnover rose dramatically', charges reduced or dismissed) [S1][S4]. And the 'proven experience' quote in the scoring basis has no cited position line in the dossier.

The direction is supported: he prioritizes repeat, violent and sex offenders [S4], and he wrote an April 2026 letter opposing misdemeanor bail caps [S9], which is a concrete enforcement-side action. But he explicitly calls himself 'an early champion of diversion and therapeutic courts' to 'stop the revolving door' [S4], a pole-b plank. With signals pointing both ways, high confidence is overstated. Keep -1 at medium. This also keeps him distinguishable from Crawford, whose enforcement framing is stronger.
